subject: China is renting the chips it cannot buy
bodyMarkdown:
If you own a broad index fund, Nvidia is probably the largest single holding in it, and this week Washington started rewriting what Nvidia's customers may do with chips they never physically receive. That sounds like a technicality. It decides whether American export controls still work.

## The loophole is a rental agreement

Reuters reported overnight that Chinese AI companies are moving to lock in rented Nvidia computing capacity at data centres outside China, citing three people familiar with the matter. The rentals run through facilities in Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore and Japan. None of it is illegal. American **export controls** restrict the physical shipment of advanced chips, so a Chinese firm that cannot import an Nvidia GPU can still log into one sitting in Kuala Lumpur and train a model on it. Reuters says the rush is driven by expectations that Washington will close the gap, sharpened by the espionage scandal around Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang that has lawmakers calling for tighter rules. Buy the compute now, the thinking goes, before the paperwork catches up.

## The rule Washington cannot quite write

Commerce has been drafting a fix since at least August, when CNBC described the cloud as the loophole left open by rules written for cargo. Reports say the draft would require licences for **Blackwell** chips, Nvidia's current top-end AI line, shipped to seven more countries including Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand, and would bar Chinese firms from renting those chips in third-country data centres. Operators owned by American companies could skip the licence if they block remote logins from China and Russia and report who their customers are and how much compute they use. The problem is authority. Export-control lawyers quoted in that reporting doubt Commerce can police remote access without new legislation. The Remote Access Security Act, which would grant the power, passed the House 369 to 22 in January and has sat in the Senate Banking Committee since.

## The physical controls leak as well

Al Jazeera reported on Wednesday that a Chinese university with military ties bought Nvidia H200 chips last month while on an American export blacklist. The Financial Times has reported that Nvidia privately tells firms renting out its chips to keep Chinese customers under 49 per cent of sales, a company policy doing work the public rules do not. Senators from both parties now want chip-tracking requirements and the AI Overwatch Act folded into the defence bill. My read is that these controls were built for a world where compute was something you owned and shipped. Renting broke that assumption, and every month the Senate sits on the bill is a month in which the cheapest route around American policy stays perfectly legal.

## The takeaway

Watch the Senate Banking Committee more closely than Commerce, because a draft rule can be announced and still lose in court, which is what the lawyers in that reporting expect without the statute behind it. If you hold Nvidia through an index fund, the 49 per cent cap and any licensing on Singapore and Malaysia would bite revenue already booked as non-China, so the exposure is larger than the China line suggests. The next hard date is whenever Commerce publishes, and nobody I read will commit to one. Until then the loophole is open, and the people using it know exactly how long they have.
